mods.m01: Introduction, principles of propulsion and engine classification
mods.m02: Gas power cycles: Carnot, Otto, Diesel, Brayton and jet-propulsion cycles
mods.m03: Refrigeration cycles and aircraft air conditioning

pool.q: Air flows through a jet engine at 30 kg/s and the fuel flow is 1 kg/s. The exhaust gases leave the nozzle at a relative velocity of 610 m/s with pressure equilibrium at the exit plane. The thrust power is 1.12×10⁶ W. The equation T·u = (ṁa+ṁf)ue·u − ṁa·u² gives the flight speed u as:
pool.e: Thrust power = (31×610)u − 30u² = 1.12×10⁶ ⇒ 30u² − 18,910u + 1.12×10⁶ = 0, two roots 564.16 and 66.18 m/s (the book prints 564.15 and 66.17). The larger root is the realistic jet cruise; the smaller one is a slow flight state with the same thrust power.

pool.q: A landing aircraft rolls at 100 mph; the idling engine consumes air at 100 lbm/s and produces an exhaust velocity of 450 ft/s. What is the forward thrust of the engine? (1 mph = 1.4667 ft/s)
pool.e: T = ṁa(Ue − U)/gc = (100/32.2)×(450 − 146.67) = 942 lbf. Forgetting the flight speed gives 1,398 lbf; adding instead of subtracting gives 1,853 lbf.

pool.q: In the same situation (100 mph, 100 lbm/s), if the exhaust is deflected 90° (zero horizontal exhaust velocity) with the mass flow kept constant, the thrust along the flight direction is:
pool.e: Horizontal Ue = 0: T = (100/32.2)×(0 − 146.67) = −455.5 lbf; the negative sign means a braking (reverse) force, which is why thrust reversers help to brake. Mind the sign: forward thrust positive, reverse negative.

pool.q: A turbojet flies at 9 km (Ta = 229.74 K, Pa = 30.8 kPa) with Ai = 0.235 m², Ae = 0.25 m², f = 0.02, Pe = 200 kPa, Ue = 600 m/s. With a constant air flow of 40 kg/s, the pressure thrust (Pe − Pa)·Ae equals:
pool.e: Pressure thrust = Ae(Pe − Pa) = 0.25×(200 − 30.8)×10³ = 42,300 N, independent of flight speed. Using Ai instead of Ae gives 39,762 N; using Pe instead of (Pe − Pa) gives 50,000 N; forgetting kPa → Pa gives 42.3 (kN, not N).

pool.q: Same engine (Example 2.3, case where the air flow follows the flight speed: ṁa = ρ·U·Ai), the net thrust at 1000 km/h is closest to:
pool.e: ρ = Pa/(R·Ta) = 0.4671 kg/m³; U = 277.78 m/s; ṁa = ρ·U·Ai = 30.49 kg/s. Momentum thrust = ṁa(1+f)Ue = 18,662 N; pressure thrust = 42,300 N; momentum drag = ṁa·U = 8,470 N. Net thrust = 52,491 N (agrees with the book formula 42,300 + 18.66U − 8.47×10⁻³U² at U = 1000). Using the fixed 40 kg/s case would give 66,780 − 11.11U = 55,670 N, wrong because the real flow is lower at altitude.

pool.q: Single-spool turbojet: exit gauge pressure 41 kPa, Ae = 0.214 m², Ue = 584 m/s, ṁ = 69.4 kg/s (fuel neglected), inlet at atmospheric pressure with U = 0. The engine thrust is:
pool.e: T = (Pe − Pa)Ae + ṁUe = 41,000×0.214 + 69.4×584 = 8,774 + 40,530 = 49,304 N (the book prints 49,304 N). Both terms must be present: momentum alone gives 40,530 N, pressure alone 8,774 N; using absolute instead of gauge pressure gives 70,987 N.

pool.q: A turbojet powers a fighter at 10 km (Ta = 223.3 K, Pa = 0.265 bar) and Ma 0.8; the exhaust leaves the nozzle at 570 m/s and 0.67 bar; Ae/ṁa = 0.006 m²·s/kg; f = 0.02. The specific thrust T/ṁa (N·s/kg) is:
With the data of Example 2.5 (T/ṁa = 584.77 N·s/kg, u = 239.6 m/s, ue = 570 m/s, f = 0.02), the propulsive efficiency by the first expression (thrust power over thrust power plus wake loss) is:
pool.e: η_p = 2(T/ṁ)u/[2(T/ṁ)u + (1+f)(ue − u)²] = 71.57 %. The second expression gives 102.3 % (> 100 %: unphysical because the nozzle is choked, Pe ≠ Pa); the third, 2u/(u+ue), is only a rough 59.19 %.

pool.q: A turbofan flies at Ma 0.9 at 33,000 ft (Ta = −50.4 °C, Pa = 26.2 kPa), BPR = 3, core flow 22.7 kg/s, f = 0.015. Cold nozzle: Pec = 55.26 kPa, uec = 339.7 m/s, Aec = 0.299 m². Hot nozzle: Peh = 32.56 kPa, ueh = 452 m/s, Aeh = 0.229 m². The engine thrust is:
pool.e: u = 0.9×√(1.4×287×222.75) = 269.3 m/s. T = ṁh[(1+f)ueh − u] + ṁc(uec − u) + Aeh(Peh − Pa) + Aec(Pec − Pa) = 4,302 + 4,798 + 1,456 + 8,689 = 19,245 N = 19.25 kN (the book prints 19.257 kN, rounding). Both nozzles are choked (Pe > Pa), so there is a pressure thrust of ≈ 10.15 kN; using Pe instead of (Pe − Pa) would give 33.08 kN.

pool.q: The Boeing 747 has four CF6 turbofans, each with thrust 24.0 kN, air flow 125 kg/s, BPR 5.0, fuel flow 0.75 kg/s, Ma 0.8, altitude 10 km (Ta = 223.2 K), heating value 42,800 kJ/kg. The fan gives 75 % of the thrust; the nozzles expand fully. The fan (cold) exit velocity is:
pool.e: U = 0.8×√(1.4×287×223.2) = 239.6 m/s. ṁc = 5/6×125 = 104.2 kg/s. T_fan = 0.75×24 = 18 kN = ṁc(uec − U) ⇒ uec = 18,000/104.2 + 239.6 = 412 m/s (book: 413). Typical slips: dividing by the core flow or by the total flow.

pool.q: For the CF6 engine above (Example 2.7; uec ≈ 413 m/s, ueh ≈ 510 m/s, U ≈ 240 m/s, ṁh = 20.8 kg/s, ṁc = 104.2 kg/s), the propulsive efficiency is:
pool.e: η_p = F·U/ΔK̇E with F·U = 5.75 MW and the power imparted to the airflow ΔK̇E = 8.07 MW ⇒ η_p = 71.3 % (book 71.2 %). Taking 2U/(U + ueh) = 64.0 % wrongly applies the single-stream formula to a turbofan; η_th = 25.13 % is the thermal efficiency, not η_p.

pool.q: Also for the CF6 engine (Example 2.7), the overall efficiency η_o = η_p·η_th is:
A Boeing 747 has L/D = 17, fuel heating value 45,000 kJ/kg, a weight ratio at the end/start of cruise of 0.673 and overall efficiency 0.35. The Breguet range (g = 9.8 m/s²) is:
pool.e: S = η_o·QR/g·(L/D)·ln(m1/m2) = 0.35×45×10⁶/9.8×17×ln(1/0.673) = 10,820 km (book 10,819 km, ln rounded to 0.396). Typical slips: using (1 − 0.673) instead of ln(1/0.673) or forgetting L/D.

pool.q: An aircraft flies 4000 km at an airspeed of 250 m/s, L/D = 10, TSFC = 0.08 kg/N/h, m1 = 50,000 kg. With a 50 m/s tail wind (Vg = 300 m/s) the fuel consumed is:
pool.e: ln(m1/m2) = S·g·TSFC/(Vg·L/D) = 4×10⁶×9.8×(0.08/3600)/(300×10) = 0.2904 ⇒ m1/m2 = 1.3369; fuel = m1(1 − m2/m1) = 12,601 kg (book ≈ 12,600). A 50 m/s head wind (Vg = 200 m/s) gives 17,655 kg (book 17,654): a head wind raises the fuel needed for the same distance.

pool.q: After touchdown the pilot applies thrust reverse. Air is sucked into the engine at 40 kg/s, f = 2.5 %, aircraft speed 80 m/s, exhaust gas speed 500 m/s, exhaust pressure equal to ambient. Assume the jet is turned fully forward. The magnitude of the reverse thrust is:
pool.e: Site assumption (the problem gives no reverser angle): full 180° reversal, so T = ṁa[(1+f)(−ue) − u]. Magnitude = 40×(1.025×500 + 80) = 23,700 N: both terms brake (reversed jet momentum and ram drag). Subtracting the flight speed as for forward thrust gives 17,300 N (wrong sign).

pool.q: Before the afterburners are turned on, an airplane is traveling at 475 mph. Twenty seconds after, it is traveling at 560 mph. The average acceleration over those 20 s (m/s²) is: (1 mph = 0.44704 m/s)
pool.e: Δv = 85 mph = 85×0.44704 = 37.998 m/s; a = Δv/Δt = 1.900 m/s². Forgetting the mph → m/s conversion gives 4.25; using the final speed instead of Δv gives 12.52.

pool.q: Same problem (475 → 560 mph in 20 s, constant acceleration): the distance the plane travels in those 20 s is:
pool.e: Constant acceleration ⇒ mean speed = (475 + 560)/2 = 517.5 mph = 231.34 m/s; s = v_mean·t = 4,627 m ≈ 2.87 mi. Using the final speed (560 mph) gives 5,007 m, the initial speed 4,247 m.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 1.1. The thermal efficiency of a Carnot cycle between T1 = 288 K and T2 = 2000 K is:
pool.e: η = 1 − T1/T2 = 1 − 288/2000 = 85.6 %. Using T1/T2 = 14.4 % is the heat rejected fraction; using T2 = 864 K (end of Brayton compression) gives 66.7 %.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 1.2. An ideal Brayton cycle has T1 = 288 K and T2 = 864 K (T3 has no effect on efficiency). The thermal efficiency is:
pool.e: η = 1 − T1/T2 = 1 − 288/864 = 66.67 %, equivalent to 1 − r_p^(−(γ−1)/γ) with r_p^((γ−1)/γ) = 3 (r_p = 46.8). Putting T3 into the formula is wrong.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 1.3. The Humphrey (constant-volume combustion) cycle with T1 = 288 K, T2 = 864 K, T3 = 2000 K, γ = 1.4, η = 1 − γ(T1/T2)[(T3/T2)^(1/γ) − 1]/[(T3/T2) − 1]. Compared with Brayton (66.67 %) at the same T1 and T2, the Humphrey efficiency is:
pool.e: T3/T2 = 2.3148; (T3/T2)^(1/γ) = 1.8212; η = 1 − 1.4×0.3333×0.8212/1.3148 = 70.85 %, above Brayton 66.67 % and below Carnot 85.6 %. Slip: using exponent γ instead of 1/γ.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 1.4. The rotor of a millimetre-scale gas turbine has a radius of 1 mm and must reach a tip speed near the speed of sound (340 m/s). The rotational speed is:
pool.e: ω = V/r = 340/0.001 = 340,000 rad/s; n = ω·60/(2π) = 3,246,761 rpm = 3.247×10⁶ rpm. Confusing rad/s with rpm gives 0.34×10⁶; forgetting 2π gives 20.40×10⁶.

pool.q: Farokhi Example 3.3. A liquid-propellant rocket consumes 200 kg/s of oxidiser and 50 kg/s of fuel; the gas leaves the nozzle at V9 = 4000 m/s and p9 = 200 kPa at sea level (p0 = 100 kPa) with an exit diameter of 2 m. The rocket gross thrust is:
pool.e: Momentum thrust = ṁ·V9 = 250×4000 = 1000 kN; pressure thrust = (p9 − p0)·A9 = 100 kPa×π×2²/4 = 314.16 kN; Fg = 1,314 kN (book 1314 kN). Omitting the pressure thrust gives 1000 kN; using p9 instead of (p9 − p0) gives 1,628 kN.

pool.q: Farokhi Example 3.4. A turbojet at takeoff (V0 ≈ 0): ṁ0 = 100 kg/s, ṁf = 2 kg/s, QR = 42,000 kJ/kg, V9 = 900 m/s. The thermal efficiency η_th = (ṁ0 + ṁf)V9²/(2ṁf·QR) is:
pool.e: η_th = 102×900²/(2×2×42,000×10³) = 49.2 % (book 49.2 %), i.e. ~51 % of the fuel energy stays in the exhaust. Takeoff thrust F ≈ ṁ9·V9 = 102×900 = 91.8 kN. Slips: using ṁ0 instead of ṁ0 + ṁf, forgetting the factor 2.

pool.q: Farokhi Example 3.5. A turbojet flies at 200 m/s and the exhaust velocity is 900 m/s. Estimate the propulsive efficiency by η_p ≈ 2/(1 + V9/V0):
pool.e: V9/V0 = 4.5; η_p = 2/(1 + 4.5) = 36.36 % (the book prints 36.3 %: truncated, not rounded). Low because the jet speed far exceeds the flight speed.

pool.q: Farokhi Example 3.6. A turbofan flies at 200 m/s with a 250 m/s exhaust speed in both nozzles. The propulsive efficiency estimated by 2/(1 + V9/V0) is:
pool.e: η_p = 2/(1 + 1.25) = 88.89 % (book 88.9 %). Against the turbojet 36.36 % that is +52.5 percentage points; the book says "52.6 % increase" but the true relative rise is 144 %. Forgetting the factor 2 in the numerator gives 55.6 %; taking V0/V9 gives 80 %.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 3.7. The capture streamtube of an engine at takeoff: speed 10 m/s at area A0 and 100 m/s at A1; p0 = 100 kPa, ρ0 = 1 kg/m³. Using the Bernoulli equation (incompressible flow), the ratio p1/p0 is:
pool.e: p1 = p0 + ½ρ(V0² − V1²) = 100,000 + 0.5×1×(10² − 100²) = 95,050 Pa ⇒ p1/p0 = 0.9505. (The capture area ratio A0/A1 = V1/V0 = 10 by continuity.) Reversing the sign gives 1.0521.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 3.8. A rocket motor burns propellant at 50 kg/s with an exhaust speed of 3500 m/s, the nozzle perfectly expanded. The specific impulse Is (s) is:
Farokhi Problem 3.13. A turboshaft engine burns fuel of heating value 42,000 kJ/kg at 1 kg/s with a thermal efficiency of 0.333. The shaft power is:
pool.e: ℘s = η_th·ṁf·QR = 0.333×1×42,000 kJ/s = 13,986 kW ≈ 14 MW. For a turboshaft the thermal efficiency is defined on shaft power (El-Sayed Eq. 2.17), not on jet kinetic energy.

pool.q: Farokhi Problem 3.17(a). A convergent nozzle is perfectly expanded with exit Mach number M8 = 1.0, exit total pressure 98 % of the inlet total pressure, inlet Mach number M7 = 0.5, A8 = 0.5 m², γ = 1.33, adiabatic flow. The inlet area A7 is:
pool.e: Continuity with constant Tt: ṁ ∝ A·pt·f(M), f(M) = M(1 + (γ−1)M²/2)^(−(γ+1)/(2(γ−1))). f(1) = 0.5832, f(0.5) = 0.4335. A7 = A8·(pt8/pt7)·f(1)/f(0.5) = 0.5×0.98×0.5832/0.4335 = 0.6592 m². Ignoring the total-pressure loss gives 0.6727 m².

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.5: an aircraft in level cruise at constant speed. Which pair of equalities holds?
pool.e: Unaccelerated level flight: horizontally T_u = F_x, vertically P = F_z (slide p.5). The other pairs match forces acting in different directions.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.7: on which principle does the airplane engine generate its propulsive force?
o: The Magnus effect on a rotating propeller
Conservation of angular momentum of the rotor
pool.e: The engine accelerates a mass of gas rearwards; the reaction of the gas on the engine is the thrust (slides pp.7–10).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 pp.8 and 10: compared with propeller propulsion ("by action"), jet propulsion ("by reaction") typically:
o: expels a small mass of air rearwards with a small acceleration
expels a large mass of air rearwards with a small acceleration
expels a small mass of air rearwards with a great acceleration
expels a large mass of air rearwards with a great acceleration
pool.e: Propeller: large air mass, little acceleration (p.8). Jet: small mass, great acceleration (p.10). The same thrust T = ṁ(ue − u) can come from large ṁ with small ue − u (high propulsive efficiency) or the opposite.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.11: aerospace engines are machines that transform:
o: propeller mechanical energy into exhaust thermal energy
the kinetic energy of the airflow into chemical energy of the fuel
the potential energy contained in fuel and air into kinetic or mechanical energy
pool.e: The gas energy E produced by burning the air–fuel mixture becomes kinetic energy E_c (jet) or mechanical energy E_m (shaft).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.12: the three transformation phases of air in most propulsion systems, in order, are:
pool.e: Air is compressed, receives fuel and burns, then expands to give kinetic and/or mechanical energy (diagram p.12). This is also the order of the Brayton cycle (chapter 2).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.13: in the classification tree, reciprocating engines and jet propulsion engines both belong to which branch?
pool.e: Both take atmospheric air as oxidiser, so they are airbreathing; the non-airbreathing branch is the rocket (pp.13–14).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.16: the four strokes of a four-stroke piston engine, in working order, are:
pool.e: Intake → Compression → Power → Exhaust (coloured discs in the figure on p.16). In a piston engine the four phases follow each other in the same cylinder; in a jet engine they occur simultaneously in different components.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 pp.18–19: under which condition is a ramjet most suitable and what is its feature?
o: efficient at low speed only; has spring-loaded one-way valves
efficient at all speeds including standstill; has an axial compressor
efficient at high speed; uses a turbine driving a propeller
efficient at high speed only; no moving mechanical parts; needs initial motion from an external source
pool.e: The ramjet compresses air by the ram effect in the inlet, so it gives net thrust only when flying fast enough; no compressor/turbine; a typical application is the BrahMos cruise missile (p.19).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.22: how does a scramjet differ from a conventional ramjet?
o: Combustion takes place while the air through the engine is still supersonic
It adds a centrifugal compressor for compression at low speed
The air is slowed to subsonic speed before combustion
It carries its own liquid oxygen for combustion
pool.e: Scramjet = Supersonic Combustion RAMJET; since the flow need not be slowed to subsonic speed it loses less at very high speeds and exceeds ramjet speeds (p.22). The "own oxygen" option is the turborocket.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.24: a turboramjet is:
o: a turbofan with an unducted fan
a turbojet and a rocket sharing the combustor
a turbojet mounted inside a ramjet; bypass flaps block the flow into the turbojet in ramjet mode
a ramjet mounted inside a turbojet; bypass flaps block the flow into the ramjet in turbojet mode
pool.e: Figure p.24: (a) bypass flaps let flow into the turbojet; (b) flaps block it in ramjet mode at high speed. Application: SR-71 Blackbird, "the world's fastest jet-powered plane: Mach 3" (p.25).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.27: the four main families in the dashed box of the gas-turbine branch are:
pool.e: Outside the box are propfan/turboprofan and advanced ducted fan. Ramjet, scramjet, pulsejet, turboramjet and turborocket are other jet-propulsion branches of the tree on p.13.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.31: in a turboprop, which component provides most of the thrust?
o: The ducted fan at the front
The propeller, driven by the turbine through a reduction gearbox
pool.e: "The propulsive force is provided by the propeller and not by a thrust nozzle" (p.31); the exhaust only evacuates burnt gas and gives a residual thrust. So the turboprop belongs to indirect reaction (p.45).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.32: the speed and altitude range where a turboprop is more efficient than a turbojet, per the slide, is:
pool.e: The propeller is efficient at lower speed with tips turning below the speed of sound; the turbojet is better at higher speed and altitude. 400–450 mph ≈ 640–720 km/h; 30,000 ft ≈ 9.1 km.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.37: the bypass ratio of a turbofan is defined as:
o: bypass flow divided by the total engine flow
bypass mass flow rate divided by the mass flow rate entering the core
core mass flow rate divided by the bypass mass flow rate
fan thrust divided by core thrust
pool.e: BPR = ṁ_c/ṁ_h (cold/hot). E.g. BPR = 5 ⇒ ṁ_c = 5/6·ṁ_a, ṁ_h = 1/6·ṁ_a. Dividing by the total flow gives a number below 1, which is not the BPR.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.37: compared with a turbojet, the two main benefits of the turbofan on the slide are:
o: lower propulsive efficiency but more thrust; higher noise
better propulsive and global efficiency; lower noise
can fly at Mach 3; needs no fuel
pool.e: A larger air mass is accelerated less, so ue is closer to u and η_p = 2/(1 + ue/u) rises (p.37); a lower jet speed reduces noise.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 pp.43–45: which engines belong to direct reaction with the whole gas energy E turned into kinetic energy E_c used for propulsion?
pool.e: p.43: all the gas energy is E_c (rockets, ramjets). p.44: the turbojet is still direct reaction but a small part becomes mechanical energy E_m (driving the compressor). p.45: turboshaft/turboprop are indirect (main part E_m).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.45: "indirect reaction propulsion" means the main part of the gas energy E is transformed into:
o: electric energy stored in a battery
mechanical energy E_m, used for propulsion through a propeller or rotor
kinetic energy E_c, used directly through the nozzle
pool.e: Turboshaft and turboprop: the main part is E_m and the rest becomes E_c (residual thrust). The turbojet is the opposite: the main part is E_c (p.44).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.46–47: the "gas generator" is:
o: the electric generator attached to the propeller shaft
the part of the engine assembly in which the thermodynamic cycle necessary to produce energy is achieved
the component that supplies compressed air to the cabin
pool.e: Gas generator = compressor + combustor + compressor turbine (figure p.46). Adding a nozzle gives a turbojet; bleeding compressed air gives a turbo-air generator; extracting shaft work gives an APU (p.47).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.47: the "turbo-air generator" and the "auxiliary power unit" differ in their output:
o: delivered compressed air (turbo-air generator) and energy for various applications (APU)
pool.e: The slide says "Delivery of air under pressure" for the turbo-air generator and "Energy used for various applications" for the APU; the APU figure shows two work arrows W1 and W2 (the slide does not explain W1 and W2).

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.48 (altitude–speed chart): from low/slow to high/fast the engines are ordered:
o: turboshaft, turboprop, turbofan (by-pass turbojet), turbojet, ramjet, rocket
turboprop, turboshaft, turbojet, turbofan, rocket, ramjet
turbojet, turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft, ramjet, rocket
rocket, ramjet, turbojet, turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft
pool.e: Helicopters (turboshaft) near the ground; turboprops lower down (below ~9 km on the chart); turbofans ~10 km (airliners); turbojets (Concorde, Rafale) higher and faster; ramjet ~25 km; rockets above ~40 km.

pool.q: Slide Ch.1 p.48 labels the tropopause ("~10–11 km") at −56 °C and 264 hPa. According to the ISA (Farokhi Appendix A), the pressure at 11 km (ISA tropopause) is:
pool.e: ISA: p(11 km) = 101,325×(216.65/288.15)^5.2559 = 22,632 Pa = 226.3 hPa; it lies between 26.50 kPa (10 km) and 19.40 kPa (12 km) of the Farokhi table. 264 hPa is the pressure at 10 km (ISA 264.4 hPa) while −56 °C is the temperature at 11 km: the slide pairs values of two different altitudes.

pool.q: A jet engine takes in 30 kg/s of air, f = 0.01, exhaust speed 500 m/s (fully expanded nozzle), flight speed 200 m/s. The net thrust is:
pool.e: T = ṁa[(1+f)ue − u] = 30×[1.01×500 − 200] = 9,150 N = 9.15 kN. Dropping f gives 9.00; forgetting the ram drag ṁa·u gives 15.15; adding u gives 21.15.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbojet thrust

pool.q: A jet engine takes in 100 kg/s of air, f = 0.01, exhaust speed 700 m/s (fully expanded nozzle), flight speed 100 m/s. The net thrust is:
pool.e: T = ṁa[(1+f)ue − u] = 100×[1.01×700 − 100] = 60,700 N = 60.70 kN. Dropping f gives 60.00; forgetting the ram drag ṁa·u gives 70.70; adding u gives 80.70.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbojet thrust

pool.q: A jet engine takes in 80 kg/s of air, f = 0.015, exhaust speed 450 m/s (fully expanded nozzle), flight speed 100 m/s. The net thrust is:
pool.e: T = ṁa[(1+f)ue − u] = 80×[1.015×450 − 100] = 28,540 N = 28.54 kN. Dropping f gives 28.00; forgetting the ram drag ṁa·u gives 36.54; adding u gives 44.54.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbojet thrust

pool.q: A jet engine takes in 60 kg/s of air, f = 0.01, exhaust speed 800 m/s (fully expanded nozzle), flight speed 100 m/s. The net thrust is:
pool.e: T = ṁa[(1+f)ue − u] = 60×[1.01×800 − 100] = 42,480 N = 42.48 kN. Dropping f gives 42.00; forgetting the ram drag ṁa·u gives 48.48; adding u gives 54.48.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbojet thrust

pool.q: An engine flies at 300 m/s with an exhaust speed of 750 m/s (fully expanded nozzle, f neglected). The propulsive efficiency η_p = 2u/(u + ue) is:
pool.e: η_p = 2×300/(300 + 750) = 57.1 %. Inverting the ratio gives 71.4 %; using u/ue gives 40.0 %. The closer ue is to u, the higher η_p (but the smaller the thrust).
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: propulsive efficiency

pool.q: An engine flies at 100 m/s with an exhaust speed of 250 m/s (fully expanded nozzle, f neglected). The propulsive efficiency η_p = 2u/(u + ue) is:
pool.e: η_p = 2×100/(100 + 250) = 57.1 %. Inverting the ratio gives 71.4 %; using u/ue gives 40.0 %. The closer ue is to u, the higher η_p (but the smaller the thrust).
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: propulsive efficiency

pool.q: An engine flies at 250 m/s with an exhaust speed of 375 m/s (fully expanded nozzle, f neglected). The propulsive efficiency η_p = 2u/(u + ue) is:
pool.e: η_p = 2×250/(250 + 375) = 80.0 %. Inverting the ratio gives 60.0 %; using u/ue gives 66.7 %. The closer ue is to u, the higher η_p (but the smaller the thrust).

pool.q: Two engines give the same thrust of 10 kN at u = 250 m/s (f neglected, fully expanded nozzle): A has ue = 375 m/s (large flow, turbofan-like), B has ue = 625 m/s (small flow, turbojet-like). The ratio η_p(A)/η_p(B) is:
pool.e: Required flows: ṁA = T/(ue − u) = 80.0 kg/s, ṁB = 26.7 kg/s. η_p(A) = 2u/(u + ueA) = 0.800, η_p(B) = 0.571 ⇒ ratio 1.400. The engine that accelerates a larger air mass by a smaller amount has the higher propulsive efficiency: this is why turbofans replaced turbojets in airliners (slides pp.8, 10, 37).
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: propulsive efficiency comparison
